name: Atlantis Paradise Island
label: Atlantis
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sir Sidney Poitier Bridge' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Sidney Poitier Bridge' (roads).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Atlantis Paradise Island'.
notes: Huge resort with the iconic Royal Towers and aquarium.

text.description:
Atlantis Paradise Island is a big ocean-themed resort on Paradise Island, and its towers rise above the island across Nassau's harbour. The resort covers 154 acres and has five hotels, including the Royal, Coral, Cove and Reef Towers. The Royal Towers opened on 11 December 1998, when the site was rebranded as Atlantis. The resort also has a waterpark, a large open-air marine habitat and a marina for yachts.

The best photo is the long view from the Sir Sidney Poitier Bridge. From the pedestrian sidewalk you look across the harbour, with the towers rising behind the water and the bridge's road span running through the frame. The Nassau skyline adds a sense of place. Guides often call this the classic Atlantis skyline view, and it is a free public walk.

Keep to the sidewalk, because this is the main road bridge to the island and traffic is close by. The resort itself is private, so don't plan on photographing from inside it. If you want a second angle, Marina Village at Atlantis puts docked yachts in the foreground with the towers and pastel buildings behind. It sits inside the resort complex, so access rules may change.
text.geographic_location: Atlantis sits on Paradise Island, the island across the harbour from central Nassau.
text.directions_text: There is no public transport information for this spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the whole resort, the harbour and the bridge span fit in one frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the bridge and skyline, and try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the towers and make them look bigger against the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Sir Sidney Poitier Bridge (pedestrian sidewalk on the Paradise Island side, looking across the harbour toward the resort). The Atlantis towers rising behind the harbour and the bridge's road span, framed by the water and the Nassau skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the towers on one of the upper grid intersections, with the water filling the lower third. Use the bridge's road span as a leading line towards the resort. If you'd like a different view, Marina Village at Atlantis gives a close-up with yachts in front of the towers, but check access first.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and towers keep their detail. Hold your phone steady against the railing or your body, and stay clear of the traffic side.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light in the morning or late afternoon usually suits the towers and water better than harsh midday sun. If you stay into dusk, night mode can help in low light, as long as you hold the phone very still.

text.access_note: The bridge sidewalk is a free public walkway, but the resort itself is private and Marina Village is inside the resort complex, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the towers and water more than harsh midday sun.

name: Paradise Island
label: Paradise Island
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fort Fincastle' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Fort Fincastle' (way/191813517): middle (45 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/32897843: large area 'Paradise Island' (6468 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Resort island across the harbour from downtown Nassau.

text.description: Paradise Island is the long, low island that lies just off Nassau's shore, across the harbour. It was called Hog Island until 1962, when the developer Huntington Hartford renamed it. Today it is best known for the Atlantis resort. The island covers about 277 hectares, and two bridges link it to New Providence: the first was built in 1966 and the second in the late 1990s. It is a good subject because the resort towers, the harbour and the boats make a clear layered scene. The best way to photograph it is from height. Fort Fincastle stands on Bennet's Hill, the highest point on New Providence, so from its top landing you look down over Nassau Harbour, with Paradise Island and the eastern approaches spread out below. The fort is a quieter, higher alternative to the usual bridge view, though it is a paid spot. On a phone, the wide view works well. Keep the horizon level, let the harbour fill the lower half of the frame, and place the island in the upper third. Zoom in a little to pick out the resort towers from the surrounding greenery. Fort Fincastle and the Queen's Staircase were listed as temporarily closed during renovation of the nearby Water Tower, so check before you go.
text.geographic_location: Paradise Island sits just off the northern shore of Nassau, across Nassau Harbour from the city centre. The viewpoint, Fort Fincastle, is on Bennet's Hill, the highest point on New Providence, looking north-east towards the island.
text.directions_text: Head for Fort Fincastle on Bennet's Hill in Nassau. If the fort is closed, the Paradise Island Bridge is the usual alternative for a view over the harbour. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole harbour scene, then try 2x-5x telephoto to pick out the resort towers. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (Top landing of the fort on Bennet's Hill, the highest point on New Providence). A broad, elevated panorama over Nassau Harbour, with Paradise Island and the eastern approaches spread out below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the horizon on the upper or lower line so it stays level. Put the harbour water in the foreground and the island across the top of the frame. A little fort wall at one edge adds depth. If you want a closer, lower view with boats passing underneath, the Paradise Island Bridge is a good alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the far shoreline to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky does not wash out. For a wider sweep of the harbour, try panorama mode and move slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try a clear morning or later in the afternoon, when the light is softer and the harbour colours look richer. Midday sun can flatten the view.

text.access_note: Fort Fincastle is a paid site and may be closed for renovation work nearby, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late-afternoon light is softer and gives richer colour over the harbour than midday sun.
Gridlines help keep the horizon level.
A fort wall at the edge of the frame can add depth to the photo.
The Paradise Island Bridge gives a lower view with boats passing underneath.

name: Cable Beach
label: Cable Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Goodman's Bay Park' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Goodman's Bay Park' (relation/17992661): middle (486 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/368706886: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cable beach' (249 m across).
notes: Resort beach strip west of Nassau.

text.description:
Cable Beach is the long sandy shoreline on the northern coast of New Providence, west of Nassau town. It runs for about two and a half miles, which is why it suits wide, simple phone photos: a pale strip of sand, calm shallow water and a line of resort buildings behind. The name is said to come from an 1892 submarine telegraph cable that linked Jupiter, Florida to Goodman's Bay. Tourism here goes back to the 1940s, and by the 1950s the area was a centre for hotel building, later promoted as the "Bahamian Riviera". That history explains the resort frontage you see today.

For the best view of the shore, start at Goodman's Bay Park, along the Cable Beach shoreline to the east of the beach's middle. It has open sand and calm water, with a more relaxed, park-like feel behind you. It is a quieter alternative to the busier resort sands, and there is room to turn and frame the sea behind your subject. Weekdays are calmer, because locals use the park heavily at other times. From here the middle of Cable Beach lies to the west, so you can shoot along the shoreline towards it.

Expect vendors and jet skis on the busier sections, and parking near Goodman's Bay can be tight. Keep the horizon level and leave plenty of sky and water in the frame. The sea and sand do most of the work.
text.geographic_location: Cable Beach is on the northern coast of New Providence Island, west of central Nassau, with resort hotels lining the shore. Goodman's Bay Park sits along the same shoreline, to the east of the beach's middle.
text.directions_text: From central Nassau, head west along the north coast to Goodman's Bay Park. Once you are on the shore, the middle of Cable Beach is about 2.4 km to the west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of sand, water and sky. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a distant hotel or a person walking at the water's edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Goodman's Bay Park (shoreline stretch along Cable Beach). Open sandy space and calm water along the Cable Beach shore, with a more relaxed, park-like feel behind it. The middle of Cable Beach is to the west, so turn that way to shoot along the shoreline.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the gridlines on and set the horizon on the upper or lower line. Keep a strip of sand in the foreground so the picture has depth. If you want the wider view of the long white-sand strip, with turquoise shallows and resort hotels behind it, Cable Beach itself is the alternative spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or sand to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the bright sand does not turn white. Try a Live Photo for gentle wave movement, or panorama for the length of the shore. Hold the phone level and sweep slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go on a weekday for a calmer park and fewer people in your frame. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday.

text.access_note: No entry fee was found for Goodman's Bay Park or the beach.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning and late afternoon light is usually softer and less harsh than midday sun.
Weekdays are likely to be quieter than weekends at Goodman's Bay Park.

name: Junkanoo Beach
label: Junkanoo Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Junkanoo Beach' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).

notes: Popular town beach just west of the cruise port.

text.description:
Junkanoo Beach is a beach in Nassau, a stretch of sand with the harbour on one side and beach bars and chair rentals along the back. It is a lively place rather than a quiet one, and that suits photography. You get turquoise water, colourful bars and a good view of the harbour lighthouse in one short walk.

The best picture is at the end of the beach that faces the lighthouse. From there the lighthouse sits against the water and sky, and if you are here late in the day the sunset light can add colour. For a second picture, turn round and look back along the shoreline. The sand, the people and the bright water fit into one frame and show what the beach is like. The Tiki Bikini Hut is a third option: the colourful bar against clear blue water, with cruise ships docked nearby.

Reports on the beach differ. Some visitors find it clean and calm, while others mention litter, rocky patches and pushy vendors. Crowds are heaviest when cruise ships are in port, so mornings or days with no ships in port are easier for clean frames. Beach bars and chair rentals can creep into your shot, so move a few steps along the sand until the lighthouse has clear water and sky around it. The exact stand-here point along the beach is approximate, so use the map as a guide and adjust on the spot.
text.geographic_location: Junkanoo Beach is in Nassau, with the harbour lighthouse in view and cruise ships docked nearby. One end of the beach faces the harbour lighthouse.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or rail stops for this spot. Once you reach the sand, walk to the end of the beach that faces the harbour lighthouse. The phone icon on the map shows the spot to aim for. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lighthouse framed against the water and sky. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you turn back to take in the shoreline, beach and turquoise water together. If your phone has a telephoto lens (2x-5x), it brings the lighthouse closer and leaves out the beach clutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the lighthouse is seen from the beach, framed against the water and sky. The exact spot along the sand is approximate, so shift a few steps until the view is clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the lighthouse on one of the vertical lines, with water in the lower part of the frame and sky above. Keep the horizon level. Beach bars and chair rentals can intrude, so crouch slightly or step sideways to keep them out. For a second picture, turn round with the ultra-wide (0.5x) and take the shoreline, crowd and turquoise water in one frame. The Tiki Bikini Hut with the cruise ships behind it is another option.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lighthouse to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour, especially near sunset. Take a few frames, because people on the sand move through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mornings or days when no cruise ships are in port should be calmer. Later in the day, sunset light is possible on the lighthouse view.

text.access_note: This looks like an open beach, but check the official site before you go for any access or facility rules.

name: Queen's Staircase
label: Queen's Staircase
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Queen's Staircase' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/374794285: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Queens Staircase' (41 m long).
notes: Historic 66-step limestone staircase carved by slaves, shaded by palms.

text.description:
The Queen's Staircase is a flight of about 65 steps cut straight into solid limestone, locally known as the 66 steps because it originally had one more. Enslaved workers, about 600 of them, carved it between 1793 and 1794 to link Fort Fincastle with the town below. It was named for Queen Victoria in the 19th century. The whole flight rises about 31 metres (102 feet), with rock walls on either side, tropical plants and trees, and water trickling down beside the steps to a pool below.

It photographs well because the walls and greenery frame the steps and lead the eye up the corridor. You don't need to climb all the way. A good spot is about halfway up the flight, looking back down. From there the steps recede between the rock walls towards the street below, and it is usually quieter than the bottom, where most visitors gather. If you want the full run of the steps with the cascade and ferns in the foreground, shoot from the base instead. From the top, the staircase falls away below you with the harbour view beyond.

The steps are steep and there is no easier route, so take your time and watch your footing while holding your phone. On cruise-ship days it can get very busy, so early morning or late afternoon is the better bet. Fort Fincastle at the top is a separate site, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Downtown Nassau, on Bennet's Hill, the highest point of the city. It is part of the Fort Fincastle Historic Complex, close to Princess Margaret Hospital and the Grosvenor campus of the University of The Bahamas.
text.directions_text: No public transport is listed for this spot, so start from Downtown Nassau and make your own way to the foot of the staircase, which leads up to Fort Fincastle, using whatever local transport or route you prefer. Ask for the Queen's Staircase or the 66 steps. Once there, walk up the flight to about halfway and you are at the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the view down the corridor. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the walls, greenery and steps all in frame in the tight space.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. On the Queen's Staircase itself, about halfway up the flight, turning round to look back down.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the steps up with the middle of the frame so the walls lead the eye down. Keep your phone level so the walls don't lean. For the full run of steps with the cascade and ferns in front, take one shot from the base. From the top you can also shoot down the gully towards the harbour.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the steps, then use the exposure slider to stop bright patches of sky from washing out the shaded walls. If people are passing, take a few shots or try a Live Photo, then pick the frame with the fewest in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when it is quieter and cruise-ship crowds are smaller.

text.access_note: The staircase is open-air and free to enter, but Fort Fincastle at the top is a separate site that may charge an entry fee or close at times, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Ultra-wide (0.5x) helps fit the walls, plants and steps into frame in a narrow gully.
Bright sky patches above a shaded gully can be overexposed, so lowering the exposure slider may help.
Visitors passing through the frame may spoil a shot, so waiting or taking several frames helps.

name: Cabbage Beach
label: Cabbage Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Casino Drive' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Casino Drive nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W116986588 (Cabbage Beach): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Long white sand beach on Paradise Island.

text.description: Cabbage Beach is a long, wide stretch of white sand beside the turquoise Atlantic, and it is one of the easiest places on the map to get a bright, simple holiday photo. The colours do most of the work: pale sand, clear blue-green water and a lot of open sky. One of the commonly used public ways down is the access path on Casino Drive, between the resort properties. It is a practical starting point if you are not staying at a resort, and from the top of the path you can shoot straight down onto the shoreline. Check the map for the exact access point before you go. If you walk along the sand, you will find quieter stretches with few people, which suit wide, uncluttered beach pictures. Nearby is the Thunderball Breakwater, a concrete wall running out into the sea with the beach behind it and the Atlantis resort at the edge of the frame. Take care there. The ground is rough, the currents are strong and you should not swim. Some areas of the beach are reserved for hotel guests, and vendors rent out chairs, so you may need to frame around loungers and umbrellas. Keep your phone dry and sand-free, and wipe the lens before you shoot, because salt haze makes pictures look soft.
text.geographic_location: Cabbage Beach is on the Atlantic, on the Nassau map, with resort properties nearby and the Thunderball Breakwater next to the Atlantis complex. The Casino Drive access path is one of the commonly used public entrances, between the resort properties.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or other public transport stops are listed for this spot, so use the map to reach Casino Drive and look for the public access path down to the sand. Check the map before you set off, as the exact access point can be hard to spot between the resort buildings. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the full sweep of sand, sea and sky. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and 2x or more to pick out the breakwater or a distant swimmer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Casino Drive (public beach access point between the resort properties). The wide white-sand shoreline and turquoise Atlantic water, shot from the public access path down onto the beach.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line so the shot is not split in half. Let the path or the line of the shore lead the eye into the picture. For a quieter alternative, walk along the sand to a stretch with few people and shoot wide. Or try the Thunderball Breakwater, with the beach stretching away behind it and Atlantis at the edge of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sea to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the sand does not turn plain white. A Live Photo can catch the waves moving. Keep the phone level so the horizon is straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is usually softer.

text.access_note: The Casino Drive path is a public beach access, but some beach areas are reserved for hotel guests, and reaching the Thunderball Breakwater may involve Atlantis, so check the official site before you go.

name: Fort Fincastle
label: Fort Fincastle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Queen's Staircase' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'The Queen's Staircase' (way/374794285): middle (41 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/191813517: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fort Fincastle' (46 m across).
notes: Ship-shaped fort and water tower with views over Nassau harbour.

text.description:
Fort Fincastle sits on top of Bennet's Hill, looking over central Nassau, Paradise Island and the eastern approaches to New Providence. Lord Dunmore had it built in 1793 to protect the town from pirates, and he named it after his second title, Viscount Fincastle. The fort is shaped like a paddle steamer. It carried a handful of cannon and a howitzer, and it also worked as a lighthouse until September 1817, when the lighthouse on Paradise Island took over.

The photo from here shows the whole flight of limestone steps with tropical greenery along one side. The steps work as a leading line that pulls the eye up towards the fort. It is a shot of the staircase rather than a full view of the fort's walls, so think of it as a scene-setter for the climb.

The fort-top view is a different picture: Nassau's harbour, Paradise Island and cruise ships, with an old cannon to frame the shot. That is the highest level of the fort, and entry there is ticketed. The fort is also often reached on foot by way of the Queen's Staircase, so the two make a natural pair. Take the staircase photo first, then decide whether to go up.
text.geographic_location: Fort Fincastle is on Bennet's Hill in the city of Nassau, on New Providence island, above the town centre and reached by Prison Lane. The Queen's Staircase stands in the same historic complex, just below the fort.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from central Nassau and head for Bennet's Hill by taxi or hired scooter. Ask for the Queen's Staircase, or for Fort Fincastle, which is reached by Prison Lane. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the full run of steps climbing towards the fort. If the staircase feels cramped and you can't fit the whole flight in, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). A touch of telephoto (2x) squeezes the steps together and makes the fort at the top look closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Queen's Staircase (foot of the staircase, looking up the full flight toward the fort). The full run of the limestone steps with tropical greenery on one side, framed as a leading line toward the fort at the top. The limestone steps and the tropical greenery along one side should fill the frame. The fort is to the north-west, at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the steps along a diagonal or the centre line, so they lead the eye up to the fort. Keep the greenery on one side as a natural border. Hold the phone low and level to keep the steps straight. If you go up into the fort, the highest level gives a wide panorama of the harbour, Paradise Island and the cruise ships, with an old cannon as a foreground frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the steps to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky behind the fort looks washed out. Use panorama only at the top of the fort, where the view is widest.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is a good choice: one guide says the light is softer and the crowds are thinner then. The steps are also shaded, which helps on a bright day.

text.access_note: The Queen's Staircase is a free outdoor viewpoint, but the fort itself is ticketed and may be closed at times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Straw Market
label: Straw Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bay St & Market St' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Bay Street and Market Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W234030239 (Straw Market): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Colourful craft market on Bay Street.

text.description:
The Straw Market is a market building on Bay Street in central Nassau. The view is the Bay Street facade from the corner, though it is worth checking on the day whether the market is best photographed from outside or inside. Seen from across the road, the facade is more attractive than many visitors expect, and the street corner frames it well. The market's entrance and the people passing by add some life to the picture. The pink and white colonial-style buildings along Bay Street make a soft, colourful backdrop, so you can include some of them for a sense of place.

Stand near the corner of Bay Street and Market Street, about 56 m south-east of the market, and look north-west towards the Bay Street frontage. Start with the default lens (1x) and keep the whole facade in the frame, entrance included. If the pavement is crowded, step back to the kerb edge, taking care with traffic, or wait a moment for a gap. Switch on the gridlines to keep the building's edges straight.

The area is at its busiest from roughly 10:00 to 15:00 on days when cruise ships are in port, so an earlier or later visit gives cleaner pictures. Inside, photography generally needs a polite word with the stallholder first, so ask before pointing your phone at people or their goods.
text.geographic_location: The Straw Market is in central Nassau, on Bay Street.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops serve Nassau, so the place to head for is the Bay Street and Market Street corner in central Nassau. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the whole facade with the entrance. If the pavement is too narrow to fit it all in, try ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the building upright in the frame so the edges don't lean. Telephoto (2x or more) is useful for a tighter shot of the entrance and signage.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Bay Street and Market Street (across from the market's Bay Street frontage). The Straw Market's Bay Street facade, framed by the street corner, with the market's entrance and passing visitors.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Fit the facade in with the corner as a natural frame, and let a few people walk through for scale. Use the gridlines to keep verticals straight. For an alternative, take a wider view along Bay Street, using the pink and white colonial-style buildings around the market as a backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. If you want a clear shot without people, take a short burst or a Live Photo and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Crowds are heaviest from roughly 10:00 to 15:00 when cruise ships are in port, so go earlier or later for a quieter street. Check which days ships are due if you can.

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from the public street, but photography inside the market generally means asking the vendors first, so check the official site before you go for anything about visiting.

name: Fort Charlotte
label: Fort Charlotte
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fort Charlotte' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/302015352: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fort Charlotte' (198 m across).
notes: Largest fort in Nassau, with moats, dungeons and cannons.

text.description:
Fort Charlotte is a British colonial fort standing on a hill above Nassau Harbour, a little west of the middle of town. It was built in the late 18th century by the colonial governor, Lord Dunmore, after the American Revolutionary War. It was never used in battle, so the stonework has had a fairly quiet life. The site is large, roughly 200 metres across, and has plenty of different views to choose from.

The best first photo is the entrance. Stand in front of the arched main gate and the fort's facade fills the frame: the arch, the towers, the cannons and the flag, seen straight on. The original drawbridge makes a strong foreground and gives the picture a proper military feel. The phone icon on the map is at the fort itself, so you can start your photos as soon as you arrive.

Once inside, there are two good alternatives. From the walls you look out over Nassau Harbour, the cruise ships at the wharf and the turquoise water, with the city spread out below. Down by the dry moat, the thick walls rise steeply and the angles make interesting compositions, and the moat can add a hint of reflection.

Aim for early morning or late afternoon, when the light shows off the texture of the stone. Photography is generally allowed, but if you are thinking of flying a drone, check the rules first, as they can be strict at historic sites.
text.geographic_location: Fort Charlotte sits on a hill on the western side of central Nassau, overlooking the harbour. It is a short distance west of downtown and the cruise ship terminal.
text.directions_text: From downtown Nassau and the cruise ship terminal, head west; the fort is about a mile away on the hill above the harbour. Some visitors find the walking route and taxi access awkward, so check your route before you go. The phone icon on the map is right in front of the arched entrance. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) in front of the gate to fit the arch, towers, drawbridge and cannons into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a straighter, more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details like the cannons, the stone blocks and the flag.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand at Fort Charlotte, in front of the arched main gate, with the drawbridge and cannons in the frame. From here the photo shows the fort's entrance facade seen straight on, with the arched gate, towers, cannons and flag.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the arch up with the centre of the frame so the facade looks balanced. Keep a cannon or part of the drawbridge in the foreground for depth. Later, try the view from the walls over the harbour and cruise ships, or the walls rising from the dry moat, as alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the stone to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the sky down slightly so it does not wash out. If the flag is moving, a Live Photo gives you a few frames to choose from.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light brings out the detail in the stone.

text.access_note: The fort grounds are a visitor site where an entry fee may be charged and the amount may vary, so check the official site or ask at the gate before you go.

name: Arawak Cay
label: Arawak Cay Fish Fry
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Arawak Cay Promenade' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Arawak Cay' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/191817556: large area 'Arawak Cay' (1522 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Colourful local seafood stalls by the water.

text.description:
Arawak Cay, also known as the Fish Fry, is a 100-acre island that was made by people. It was built in 1969 from material dredged out of Nassau Harbour. Shipping began here in the 1980s, and Nassau Container Port was added in 2011. Today most visitors come for the local eateries along West Bay Street.

For photographs there are two good sides to it. The flat waterfront promenade looks over the harbour and nearby islands, and at sunset the sky can turn orange and pink. It is also a quieter option than the food-stall strip. The other side is Arawak Cay Beach, where rows of colourful painted vendor stalls fill the foreground, with piles of conch shells and the harbour and skyline behind them.

The stalls and restaurants are busy at weekends and after dark. If you want clean shots without crowds in them, go at a quieter time. Use the promenade for wide, open views of water and sky. Save the stall-lined area for close, colourful frames. Keep your phone steady against your body or a railing, and take a few shots of each scene so you can pick the sharpest.
text.geographic_location: Arawak Cay lies along West Bay Street, just west of Junkanoo Beach, about 15 minutes from downtown Nassau. It is the long man-made island that holds the Fish Fry eateries and the container port.
text.directions_text: Start from downtown Nassau, which is about 15 minutes away. Head west along West Bay Street towards Junkanoo Beach, then carry on a little further. The cay is reached from Arawak Cay Drive and Fish Fry Way. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of harbour and sky. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the water and islands. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single island or a boat against the colour in the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Arawak Cay Promenade (western part of the cay). The harbour and nearby islands from the waterfront path, with the sky lit in orange and pink at sunset.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line. Give more room to the sky when the colours are strong, and more to the water when it is calm. Include a bit of the path or railing in the foreground to give the picture depth. For a different shot, Arawak Cay Beach has rows of painted vendor stalls with conch shells in front and the harbour and skyline behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset colours do not wash out. As the light fades, switch on night mode and hold the phone still against a railing or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, for the colour in the sky. Choose a quieter time than weekends or after dark if you want the stalls and path less crowded.

text.access_note: The promenade is a public waterfront path, but this is a working port area, so check the official site before you go for any restrictions.
claims_not_in_sources: The waterfront path is a public, free-to-walk space.
Holding the phone against a railing or your body helps keep night shots steady.
The sky colours at sunset are strongest when the sky is fairly clear.

name: Fort Montagu
label: Fort Montagu
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Montagu Beach' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Montagu Beach' (relation/17982883): middle (435 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/191808714: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fort Montagu' (34 m across).
notes: Oldest fort in Nassau, guarding the eastern harbour entrance.

text.description: Fort Montagu is a small limestone fort on the eastern shore of New Providence Island, at the eastern end of Nassau. It has just four cannon today. Work began in 1741 under the military engineer Peter Henry Bruce, to guard the island against Spanish attack, and it was finished the following year. It later played a part in the American Revolutionary War, when American forces took it before moving on to Nassau itself. The fort is low and compact, so it is easy to fit into a phone frame. The best view is from the beach in front of it, where the walls rise above the sand. Behind them you can see the harbour and the resort buildings across the water, and the view toward Paradise Island is a popular extra shot. Start with a wide shot that includes sand, walls and sky, then move in for a closer frame of the stonework. Keep the horizon level using your gridlines. The fort grounds and any tour inside may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go. Seaweed has been reported on the beach on some visits, so look at the sand before you frame your shot.
text.geographic_location: Fort Montagu stands on the eastern shore of New Providence Island, at the eastern end of Nassau Harbour. Montagu Beach lies directly in front of it.
text.directions_text: Head east along the harbour shore from central Nassau to Montagu Beach. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the beach, the walls and the sky together. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the fort. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the stonework or boats on the harbour.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Montagu Beach (beach in front of the fort, looking back at the walls). The fort's walls rising above the beach, with the harbour and resort buildings across the water in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the horizon on a gridline and keep the fort walls on one third, with some sand in the foreground. For a second angle, walk closer and photograph the limestone fort with Nassau Harbour, passing boats and the turquoise water behind it. A shot across the harbour toward Paradise Island also works.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky and water keep their colour. Use portrait mode if you want a person on the sand with the fort softly blurred behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Afternoon is likely to suit this view, because the sun should then be behind you and light the walls. Early morning may put the fort against the light.

text.access_note: The beach is an open public space, but the fort and any tour inside may have their own admission and opening rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Facing east from the beach, afternoon sun comes from behind the photographer and lights the fort walls, while morning sun is behind the fort.
Gridlines, the exposure slider and portrait mode will help with this kind of scene.

name: Ardastra Gardens
label: Ardastra Gardens
camera_source: Commons cluster (10 photos). Moved 91 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 250 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/304215080: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ardastra Gardens, Zoo & Conservation Centre' (254 m across).
notes: Zoo famous for its marching flamingos.

text.description: Ardastra Gardens, Zoo and Conservation Centre is a garden zoo in Nassau, best known for its flamingos. It opened in 1937, the work of the Jamaican horticulturist Hedley Vivian Edwards. The name comes from the Latin Ardua astrum, meaning "Striving for the stars". The flamingos arrived in the 1950s, when the Bahamian government brought them in to breed because they had become rare locally. Today the zoo holds about 200 animals. It suits a phone camera because the subjects are bright, colourful and often close, and the planted gardens give a green backdrop. The gardens cover an area roughly 250 metres across, so there is room to move around for different angles. Flamingos tend to stand in groups, so look for a clean line of birds with the planting behind them. Wait for a moment when a bird lifts its head or stretches its wings rather than taking the first frame you see. Fences and mesh can creep into the shot, so move to a gap or hold the phone close to the barrier.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed near here, so check local transport options for getting to the gardens from central Nassau. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wider garden scenes and groups of birds. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for single flamingos and other animals, so you can stay back and still fill the frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only for broad planted areas or paths, as it makes distant animals look tiny.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (inside the garden, in the arena seating area). Marching Caribbean flamingos walking up to the crowd, with the keeper and the arena setting in the frame. Inside, pick a spot with an open view of the flamingos and keep the sun behind or beside you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the birds on a third of the frame, leaving space in the direction they are looking. Hold the phone close to the fence or mesh so it blurs out of the picture. Take a few frames of the same group, as the birds keep shifting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the nearest bird's head to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the pink and orange feathers stay rich and not washed out. Live Photos or motion can help catch a wing stretch, but pick a still frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or later in the afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows than midday. Check the official site for visiting times before you go.

text.access_note: This is a zoo and garden attraction that is probably ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Flamingos stand in groups and are pink or orange in colour.
Fences or mesh may appear in photos of the animals.
Morning or later afternoon light is usually softer than midday light.
The attraction may require a ticket for entry.

name: Government House
label: Government House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Duke Street & George Street corner' (4 web pages); placed at crossing of Duke Street and George Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/371290296: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Government House' (107 m across).
notes: Pink colonial residence of the Governor-General with a Columbus statue.

text.description: Government House is the official residence of the Bahamas' governor-general, and it sits on a hill above downtown Nassau. The walls are a bright conch-pink with white trim, which looks cheerful on a phone screen, and the central entrance has a pediment held up by four stout Ionic columns. The house was completed in 1806 on a rise known as Mount Fitzwilliam, and it is often called the country's finest example of Georgian Colonial building. The columned front you see today dates from the 1930s, when the house was remodelled after the hurricane of 1929. In front stands a 12-foot statue of Christopher Columbus, placed there in 1830. It is a controversial figure, so think about whether you want it in the frame. The best view is from the corner of Duke Street and George Street, on the uphill approach. From there you can fit the whole pink-and-white front, the columns, the circular drive and the statue into one picture without going through any gate. This matters because the house is a working residence, and the grounds are not always open to visitors. If you would like a different angle, the forecourt gives a closer view when it is open. Parliament Square is a quieter fallback, with a wider view of the pink Parliament and Supreme Court buildings, but it does not show the house itself.
text.geographic_location: Government House is on Duke Street, on a hill overlooking downtown Nassau and the harbour. It stands a short walk uphill from Parliament Square.
text.directions_text: Start from downtown Nassau, around Parliament Square, and walk uphill towards the house on Duke Street. If you are coming from further away, head for Duke Street and ask for Government House. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the whole front, the columns and the Columbus statue into one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the pavement is too narrow to step back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the pediment, columns and cupola-topped roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Duke Street and George Street (corner on the uphill approach, facing the front of the house). The pink-and-white Georgian facade, its columns and circular drive, with the Columbus statue in front of the building. Face south towards the front of the house.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the columns upright, so the front looks straight rather than leaning. Put the statue low in the frame and the pediment near the top third. If you want a different view, the forecourt shows the house with the statue in the foreground, when it is open. Parliament Square gives a wider, calmer shot of the nearby pink government buildings, but not a direct view of the house.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pink wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the white trim or the sky starts to glow. Stay behind the gate line and keep to the public street.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning and late afternoon light suit the building best, according to a photography guide.

text.access_note: This is a working residence, and access to the grounds is limited and can change, so check the official site before you go; the street corner is the safe default.
claims_not_in_sources: Strong midday sun can wash out pale pink and white walls, so exposure may need adjusting.
The pavement at the street corner may be narrow, which is why ultra-wide is suggested only as a fallback.
The stand-here point is on the north side of the house, based on the map data (the house lies to the south of it).

name: St. Andrew's Presbyterian Kirk
label: St Andrew's Kirk
camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak. Moved 31 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 75 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/408486495: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Andrews Presbyterian Kirk' (36 m across).
notes: Historic Presbyterian church near Government House.

text.description:
St. Andrew's Presbyterian Kirk is a historic church in downtown Nassau. It began in 1798 when fifty-five Scottish Presbyterian settlers formed the St. Andrew Society. The congregation first met in the Court House, with services starting in January 1810, and the foundation stone of the kirk itself was laid on 7 August 1810. A session room was added in 1842 to make space for a growing congregation.

It works well as a phone subject because it is a solid, characterful building among the streets of downtown, so you can take a straightforward picture of the whole front and then move in for details such as the doorway, windows and stonework. Keep your phone upright for the full height of the building, and turn it sideways if you want to include the neighbouring buildings and street.

The church is still a working congregation, so be considerate if a service is under way. Inside there are two stained glass windows either side of the communion table, but check the official site before you go to find out whether visitors can go in.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Nassau, Bahamas. The first manse was started in the 1890s on East Hill Street above the Kirk.
text.directions_text: Make your way to downtown Nassau and look for St. Andrew's Presbyterian Kirk; there are no nearby rail or tram stops to list. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building as you see it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the street is narrow and you cannot fit the front in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for doorway, window and stonework details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Prince's Street and Peck's Slope (opposite the Central Bank building). The Gothic front of the Kirk with its tower, seen from across Prince's Street. Stay on the pavement and keep clear of traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the church's vertical edges with them so the walls do not lean inwards. Keep the building in the middle third and leave a little sky above the roof. If you move closer, try a second shot of the entrance on its own.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail and the sky does not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the walls than the middle of the day, when shadows are harsh and the sky can look washed out.

text.access_note: The kirk is an active place of worship, so dress respectfully and check the official site before you go to see whether you can go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The kirk can be photographed well from the stand-here point outside, without entering.
Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and warmer than midday light.
The kirk is a working church, so visiting may be limited during services and interior access should be checked.
The stand-here point lies on a pavement or street where traffic may pass.

name: Christ Church Cathedral
label: Christ Church Cathedra
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'West Hill Street' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of West Hill Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W444246696 (Christ Church Cathedral): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Christ Church Cathedral is a church in the middle of Nassau, and the reason it photographs so well is what stands behind it. From the right street you can line the cathedral up against the pink government buildings, and with a clear blue sky above, the colours do a lot of the work for you. That pairing is the classic way to picture the building.

A travel guide singles out West Hill Street for this view. It is an ordinary public street, so you can take your time, but keep an eye out for passing traffic and other people. If you want a different feel, Rawson Square gives you the cathedral from the open downtown plaza, with everyday street life around it.

A phone copes well here. Hold it level, let the pink buildings sit behind the cathedral, and give the sky a good share of the frame so the blue comes through. Take one wide shot to show the whole scene and one closer shot of the cathedral on its own.

If you plan to go inside, photography in the church may be restricted, so confirm the policy first. Opening hours and possible closures should also be checked before you visit.
text.geographic_location: Christ Church Cathedral is in central downtown Nassau, with the pink government buildings behind it. Rawson Square, the open plaza in the centre of town, is the other good place to see it from.
text.directions_text: There is no nearby station or stop to start from, so make your way on foot from central Nassau to West Hill Street. Rawson Square is the alternative viewpoint if you are already in the middle of town. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the cathedral together with the pink buildings behind it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want to include more of the street and sky, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the cathedral against the pink backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on West Hill Street. The cathedral framed against the pink government buildings behind it, with blue sky giving strong colour contrast.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the cathedral up on one of the vertical lines so the building stands straight. Leave the pink buildings visible behind it and keep some blue sky at the top. As an alternative, Rawson Square shows the cathedral from the open plaza with downtown street life around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cathedral to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky looks washed out. This keeps the blue deep and the pink buildings rich.

text.access_note: West Hill Street is a public street, but access to the cathedral itself, opening hours and any photography rules inside may vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the phone level and using the gridlines helps keep the cathedral's vertical lines straight.
Lowering the exposure slider slightly can keep a bright sky looking blue.
Traffic and other people may pass along West Hill Street.

name: St. Francis Xavier Cathedral
label: St. Francis Xavier
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'West Street and West Hill Street corner' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of West Street and West Hill Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q23754896: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Catholic cathedral on West Hill Street.

text.description: St. Francis Xavier Cathedral is the mother church of The Bahamas and the seat of the Catholic Archdiocese of Nassau. It photographs well because the historic facade and entrance, topped by a tall steeple, stand out clearly against the tropical sky. The story behind it is easy to put in a caption. The first Mass was celebrated in November 1886 and the church was dedicated to St. Francis Xavier in February 1887. It was the first Catholic church in the Bahamas. Transepts were added in 1899, and the southern extension and two towers were completed in 1934. It became a cathedral in 1960. A newer cathedral building was dedicated in 2004, just 17 metres from the original church, and the old building is still in use. That means two churches can end up in one frame, so decide whether you want the old facade on its own or the pair together. One visitor describes the church as sitting at the top of a steep street, which can make a straight-on shot tricky. Take a few steps to each side and compare. For the classic front view, try the corner of West Street and West Hill Street. Keep the steeple and entrance in the same picture and give the sky some space above. If you go inside, photos for personal use are generally fine, but avoid flash during services.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is on West Street in Nassau, near the National Art Gallery of The Bahamas. The new cathedral building was dedicated just 17 metres from the original church.
text.directions_text: Head for West Street in Nassau, close to the National Art Gallery of The Bahamas. The West Street and West Hill Street corner is a good area for the front view, not the exact stand-here location. Once you arrive, look for the steeple above the entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade and entrance. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too tight to fit the steeple in. Use telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for the steeple and entrance details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of West Street and West Hill Street (at the cathedral's main street frontage, where the historic facade and entrance face the street). The cathedral's historic facade and entrance with its tall steeple, framed against the tropical sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the entrance up with the centre of the frame, with the steeple above it. The street slopes, so check that the building doesn't look tilted. If the newer cathedral building appears behind, decide whether to include it or move a step or two to leave it out.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright sky is washing out the sky and steeple. Inside, turn the flash off, and use night mode only if you can hold the phone steady and no service is under way.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning light is suggested for the exterior. Midday is better if you want to photograph the stained glass inside.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a working place of worship with regular services, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and any rules on photography.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting a phone upwards, or using the ultra-wide lens up close, can make a tall building look as if it leans.
A slightly lower exposure can stop a bright sky from washing out the steeple.

name: Versailles Gardens
label: Versailles Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'French Cloister at Versailles Gardens' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q24297157: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Terraced gardens with a relocated French cloister and statues.

text.description:
Versailles Gardens is on Paradise Island, beside Nassau Harbour. Its centrepiece is a stone cloister: a row of arches and columns with no roof, which looks as if it belongs somewhere in Europe rather than the Caribbean. That is close to the truth. The cloister is said to come from a European Augustinian monastery, which was taken apart, shipped over and later rebuilt stone by stone here. Its age is given as anything from the 12th to the 14th century. It looks out to Nassau Harbour on one side and the Ocean Club resort on the other.

The place photographs well because the stonework gives you a strong frame. The arches repeat, so the eye is led along them, and the harbour water shows through the openings behind the stone. Beyond the cloister, the formal garden has a long central path, steps, a pond and statues, which suit tall photos with clear lines.

For the best phone picture, stand on the cloister steps and look out towards the harbour, so the arches sit in the foreground and the water behind them. Take a few frames in both portrait and landscape orientation. If other visitors wander through, wait a moment for a gap. The cloister is popular with wedding and engagement photographers, so it can be busy at times. Access rules can vary, so check access on arrival.
text.geographic_location: On Paradise Island, beside Nassau Harbour, in the grounds next to the Ocean Club resort. The cloister looks over Nassau Harbour on one side.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed near this spot. It is on Paradise Island, next to the Ocean Club resort. Walk into the gardens and head for the stone cloister; the phone icon on the map is at the cloister itself, so there is no further walk once you arrive. Check access on arrival, as the rules may differ. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the steps to fit the whole row of arches in, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of the columns or a single arch with the water behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the roofless stone arches and columns fill the foreground and the harbour water shows through the openings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the arches look straight. Keep the harbour in the gap between two columns, and let the nearest arch frame the shot. For a second picture, try the formal garden's long central path leading up to the pond and statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright water is washing out. Try a Live Photo if people are passing, so you can choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning for fewer people and softer light, or late afternoon for warmer light on the stone.

text.access_note: Access is not clear: the cloister may be free and open to the public, or it may be limited to Ocean Club guests, so check access on arrival and follow any staff instructions.

name: Bay Street
label: Bay Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parliament Square' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parliament Square' (relation/14900727): middle (36 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q18170136: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Main shopping street along the harbour in downtown Nassau.

text.description: Bay Street is a major street in Nassau and a centre for politics, business, culture and tourism in The Bahamas. When the town was founded, somewhere between 1648 and 1666, the street was known as "The Strand". That history sits alongside today's souvenir stalls and shopfronts, so a photo here can show old and new at once. For a phone photo, the best-looking stretch is at Parliament Square. There, the pink-and-white government buildings and the marble Queen Victoria statue are framed against the street, with Bay Street running past close by. The statue gives the picture a clear centre, and the pastel buildings behind it add colour without any fuss. Bay Street is also where cruise ships send large numbers of visitors, so it can be busy, and you may have to wait a moment for a clear view. Start with the statue in the foreground and the buildings behind. Then turn to the street itself for a second shot showing the shops and passers-by. If you want a different view, the colourful front of the Nassau Straw Market, also on Bay Street, makes a good alternative. Keep your phone steady against your body, check the corners of the frame for stray bags and signs, and take a few frames so you have a clean one to choose from.

text.description: The Bahamian Parliament Building is the home of the House of Assembly, set on Parliament Square on Bay Street in Nassau. The complex was built in 1815 by Loyalist refugees from the newly independent United States, in a British colonial style often compared with American Federal architecture. Its coral-pink walls, together with the Senate building beside it, are what make it so easy to photograph: the colour stands out against blue sky and green palms. A marble statue of Queen Victoria stands in the square and makes a natural foreground. Face south with the statue low in the frame and the pink facades and palms behind it. The square is busy on weekdays and when cruise ships are in, so be patient and wait for a gap in the crowd, or shoot a little wider and accept some people in the picture. Construction equipment has sometimes appeared nearby, so check the edges of your frame before you press the shutter. Stick to the exterior: photography inside is usually not allowed, and the building may be off-limits to photographers on some days. If you have time, the Royal Victoria Garden gives a softer, leafier view of the same building.
text.geographic_location: In Nassau, on Parliament Square, Bay Street. The square is a short walk from the cruise port.
text.directions_text: Head for Parliament Square on Bay Street in downtown Nassau. From the cruise port it is a short walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the statue and the pink facades sit together without distortion. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is crowded and you want to fit in more of the buildings. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the statue or the rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parliament Square (in front of the Senate building, with the Queen Victoria statue as the foreground). The pink colonial Senate and House of Assembly buildings framed by palms, with the marble Queen Victoria statue in front of the Senate.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the statue on one of the lower third points, with the pink walls filling the middle and the palms at the sides. Keep your phone level so the buildings do not lean. For a different view, the Royal Victoria Garden shows the building's rear and facade framed by garden foliage and flowers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pink wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the colour stays rich and the sky does not wash out. Check the edges of the frame for people and building equipment before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the pink walls look their best. Weekdays and cruise-ship days are busier, and a parade is sometimes held around 9-10am, which may add people to your shot.

text.access_note: Photograph the exterior only; access to the building itself may be restricted on some days.
claims_not_in_sources: Dragging the exposure slider down slightly helps keep the pink walls rich and stops the sky washing out.
